option: Godot 4 (4.6.x stable, mid-2026) — GDScript or C#, 2D Compatibility/Forward+ renderer
oneLine: Godot 4 absolutely deserves a slot on the list — it is the only candidate with two shipped 10M-copy games in exactly this genre and a $0/no-royalty license — but hitting 2,000 entities means bypassing the node system that is Godot's whole selling point, and you must choose between C# (fast enough for the 100x balance harness, but literally cannot export to web) and GDScript (web works, several times slower on the hot loop).
strengths: Genre precedent is unmatched: Brotato (10M+ copies) and Halls of Torment are both Godot horde-survival/bullet-heaven games. No other engine on a shortlist has two direct comparables at this scale. Halls of Torment additionally shipped Windows/Linux/Android/iOS/PS5/Xbox — the whole publishing path is proven by a game in this exact genre.

MIT license, zero royalties, zero revenue share, zero seat fees — only an attribution notice in credits. For a game whose monetization fantasy is a gacha meta-layer, this is materially better than Unity's historical terms, and you keep full copyright of your content.

Genuine dedicated 2D renderer, not an orthographic 3D camera. Godot's CanvasItem pipeline has its own coordinate system, its own batching (rects sharing texture/material/blend/shader batch together), 2D-native lighting (Light2D/CanvasModulate), Y-sort, canvas_item-space shaders, and integer-scaling stretch modes. Concretely for this game: 4000x4000px world coords are just world coords (no 1-unit-per-100-pixel fiction), CanvasLayer gives you a HUD that ignores the camera for free, and a 2D shader operates on the sprite, not a quad in a 3D scene.

The spec's architecture is already the Godot-optimal architecture. Object pools + entity arrays + hand-rolled 64px spatial hash + a single render pass is precisely what Godot's own docs prescribe for thousands of instances. You are not fighting the engine; you are skipping the part of the engine that would fight you.

Two hard spec requirements come free. Fixed 60Hz timestep with interpolated rendering is engine-native (_physics_process at physics_ticks_per_second=60 + 2D physics interpolation, in-engine since 4.3) — delete your hand-rolled accumulator. And `--headless` with a dummy display/audio driver is a built-in flag on the standard binary, no separate build needed, plus `--disable-render-loop` so you can drive your own sim clock.

Entire project is agent-authorable plain text: .gd, .tscn, .tres, project.godot, export_presets.cfg. Godot publishes a formal TSCN file-format spec. The only generated artifacts (.import sidecars) are rebuilt by one CLI command, `godot --headless --import`. An AI agent never needs to touch a GUI.

GDScript is a small, consistent, Python-shaped API surface (~850 built-in classes) that LLMs hallucinate against less than Unity's sprawling, version-fragmented API. Godot 4.6 also landed bytecode optimizations to array iteration, dictionary access, and method-call overhead — the exact three operations a 2,000-entity loop lives on.
Godot's Control-node UI system is a real strength for the menu-heavy half of this game (hub, gacha screen, roster, level-up cards, results, codex), and those .tscn trees are hand-writable text.

Escape hatch exists if GDScript stalls: BlastBullets2D is a free open-source C++ GDExtension using multimesh + a sparse set, targets Godot 4.5/4.6, compiles for Windows/macOS/Linux/Android/iOS AND web. You can drop native performance into the hot loop without abandoning the project.
dealbreakers: HARD BLOCK if you want C# and a web build: official docs state flatly, 'Projects written in C# using Godot 4 currently cannot be exported to the web.' The cause is architectural — the .NET runtime can only be built as a WASM main module, and Godot's WASM already is the main module. Prototypes and community forks exist (ComplexRobot/godot-dotnet-web-export), but it is unsupported in 2026. You must pick: fast language OR browser build.

Acceptance criterion #1 in the spec — 'Opens from index.html with no build step and no network requests' — dies permanently. An EMPTY Godot 4 web project ships roughly 35MB of compressed WASM (about 25MB with aggressive stripping) before a single character exists. That is not a browser-instant game; it is a 30-second download. If zero-install, click-a-link distribution is genuinely non-negotiable, Godot cannot deliver it and no amount of optimization changes the floor.

The 100x headless balance harness is the single requirement most likely to fail, and it fails specifically in GDScript. 100x speed x 60Hz x 2,000 entities = ~12M entity-updates/sec, across 19 characters x 7 stages. C# handles that; GDScript almost certainly will not. If you choose GDScript for the web build, expect to settle for ~10-30x, or to maintain a second C#/GDExtension sim implementation — which then risks the harness and the shipped game diverging, defeating the harness's entire purpose.

To hit 2,000 entities you must NOT use nodes — no Node2D, CharacterBody2D, or Area2D per entity. That means Godot's editor cannot visualize your enemies, the remote scene tree debugger shows you nothing, and the vast majority of Godot tutorials, docs, forum answers, and LLM training data (all node-centric) stop applying to ~60% of your codebase. You are using Godot as a windowing/audio/input/export/UI layer while writing the simulation yourself, in a language slower than V8.

Web export is WebGL 2.0 / Compatibility renderer only (Forward+ and Mobile are unsupported pending WebGPU), single-threaded by default, with documented Safari WebGL 2.0 problems, background-tab pausing, and audio-autoplay restrictions. Godot's own docs state native builds outperform web 'by a significant margin.'

facts.claim: Godot Engine is MIT-licensed with no royalties, no revenue share, and no fees for commercial use; the only obligation is including the copyright notice/license statement in documentation or credits. Godot's license does not apply to your game content — you retain full copyright.

C# projects in Godot 4 cannot be exported to the web. Official docs: 'Projects written in C# using Godot 4 currently cannot be exported to the web.' Root cause: the .NET runtime can only build as a WASM main module, and Godot's WASM is already the main module (no dynamic linking).

Godot 4 web export targets WebGL 2.0 only via the Compatibility rendering method; Forward+ and Mobile are unsupported on web. Single-threaded export is now the default and recommended mode; threaded export requires SharedArrayBuffer plus Cross-Origin-Opener-Policy: same-origin and Cross-Origin-Embedder-Policy: require-corp headers.

Godot's docs explicitly recommend bypassing the scene/node system via the RenderingServer and PhysicsServer APIs for large instance counts: 'the whole scene system is optional... it can be completely bypassed.' The 2D calls are RenderingServer.canvas_item_create(), canvas_item_set_parent(), canvas_item_add_texture_rect(), canvas_item_set_transform(). Critical gotcha: RID references are not refcounted — you must keep a reference to the resource outside the server or it gets freed.
PhysicsServer2D objects can be created and manipulated independently of the scene tree — physics bodies do not have to be tied to nodes.

2D physics interpolation (fixed timestep sim with interpolated rendering) is built into the engine, implemented for 2D since Godot 4.3, and documented as of 4.4. Move objects and the camera in _physics_process to use it.

Godot 4.x ships headless mode in the standard binary via --headless (dummy display server + audio driver); no separate headless build is required. Common CI invocation: godot --headless -d --display-driver headless --audio-driver Dummy --disable-render-loop --path . -s res://script.gd

Brotato is built entirely in Godot (Godot 3), was developer Thomas Gervraud's (Blobfish) first Godot game, sold 1M+ copies in early access and 10M+ by 2025. It is featured on Godot's official showcase.

Halls of Torment (Chasing Carrots) is a Godot-built horde-survival/bullet-heaven game, 1.0 released Sept 2024 on Windows/Linux, ported to Android and iOS Oct 2024, and to PlayStation 5 and Xbox Oct 2025. It is on Godot's official showcase. This is the strongest proof that the full publishing path — desktop, mobile, and console — works for this exact genre on this exact engine.
Godot 4.6.3 is the current stable release (May 2026); 4.6 shipped Jan 2026 with Jolt physics as default. Godot 4.7 entered beta April 24, 2026 with 1,265 fixes from 309 contributors.

Concrete 2D entity-count data point: a bullet-hell devlog reports moving from per-bullet nodes (~230ms per physics step spawning 20 bullets/0.1s) to PhysicsServer2D shapes on a single shared Area2D plus direct _draw() texture calls, reaching ~240 FPS with 2,500 bullets on integrated-GPU hardware, versus under 80 FPS before. This is the closest real-world measurement to the 2,000-entity target.
facts.source: https://worldeater-dev.itch.io/bittersweet-birthday/devlog/210789/howto-drawing-a-metric-ton-of-bullets-in-godot (numbers partly from an author comment, single source, Godot 3-era)

facts.claim: Drawing ~1000 sprites via RenderingServer canvas items directly (array of RIDs + canvas_item_set_transform per frame) is substantially faster than 1000 Sprite2D nodes; MultiMeshInstance2D is GPU-instanced to one draw call regardless of instance count. Tradeoff: harder to read/debug, and the editor cannot visualize the entities.
facts.source: docs.godotengine.org/en/stable/tutorials/performance/using_multimesh.html; Godot forum threads on RenderingServer canvas items; golden-tamarin.com/2024/10/08/godot-renderingserver/

facts.claim: C# is on the order of several times faster than typed GDScript on compute-bound work (tight numerical loops, large array processing, custom physics) — the gap widens specifically for 'large-scale agent simulation with hundreds-to-thousands of complex per-frame state updates.' Godot 4.6 narrowed the gap with bytecode optimizations to array iteration, dictionary access, and method-call overhead, most pronounced for typed GDScript.

Statically-typed GDScript runs up to 59% faster than untyped GDScript on vector operations, because typed instructions let the VM skip runtime type checks. Static typing is therefore mandatory, not optional, for this project.

An empty Godot 4.4 web project delivers roughly 35MB of compressed WASM, reducible to about 25MB with asset-pack stripping. Basis Universal texture compression cuts asset size further by transcoding to GPU formats at runtime. Long web sessions can leak memory (WASM heap is not cleaned aggressively), reportedly a non-issue under ~30 minutes of playtime — note this game targets 15-25 minute runs plus meta screens, which sits right at that boundary.

.gd, .tscn, .tres, project.godot and export_presets.cfg are all human-readable plain text with a documented format, fully version-controllable and directly authorable by an LLM without any conversion step. Generated .import sidecars are rebuilt by `godot --headless --import`, so a pure text-in/CLI-out workflow with no GUI is viable. Caveat: the headless import step is known to be flaky in CI and can exit non-zero even on success.

Console publishing: W4 Games sells official middleware export templates for Nintendo Switch, Switch 2 (early beta as of early 2026), Xbox Series X|S and PlayStation 5, optimized for Godot 4.3+, with per-title/per-platform quotes and no public pricing. Pineapple Works and Lone Wolf offer port-for-hire. RAWRLAB Games released a free Godot port for authorized Nintendo Switch/Switch 2 developers.

Steam integration is solved by GodotSteam (open-source GDExtension for Windows/macOS/Linux) or Godot.Steamworks.NET for C#. GodotSteam 4.14+ auto-syncs stats/achievements at boot with no explicit request/callback needed. Steam imposes no engine restrictions.

Godot 4 supports CBDT/CBLC (embedded-PNG) and SVG color emoji fonts but NOT COLR/CPAL vector emoji fonts. CBDT fonts blur when rendered above their embedded PNG size. Emoji require bundling a font (e.g. Noto Color Emoji) or loading a system font, with fallback configured in the base font's import options.

BlastBullets2D is a free, open-source C++ GDExtension using a multimesh-based system with an internal dynamic sparse set, claiming 'THOUSANDS of bullets visible on screen.' It targets Godot 4.5 and 4.6 and ships compiled for Windows, macOS, Linux, Android, iOS and Web.

Godot's 2D engine is a purpose-built pipeline with its own physics, lighting and coordinate system rather than a layer over the 3D renderer. Unity's 2D mode locks the z-axis of a 3D orthographic camera; Unreal's 2D support (Paper2D/Slate) is not a first-class rendering path. This is a widely-repeated characterization across engine comparisons rather than a single vendor benchmark.

A widely-cited claim that Godot 'chokes at 50 simultaneous enemies' by default, rising to ~200 with the Jolt physics plugin, comes from one blog post about a specific CharacterBody2D-based Vampire Survivors starter kit. Directionally correct about naive node+physics approaches, but the exact numbers should not be trusted as an engine ceiling.

For a 100x headless sim, the engine-level approach is scaling Engine.time_scale, Engine.physics_ticks_per_second and Engine.max_physics_steps_per_frame together (e.g. 100.0 / 6000 / 800). Godot's own docs warn that time_scale above 1.0 makes physics less precise as each tick stretches over more engine time — which is why a deterministic manual sim loop (--disable-render-loop and step your own fixed clock) is the correct pattern here, not time_scale.
facts.source: docs.godotengine.org/en/stable/classes/class_engine.html; Godot forum 'Docs clarification regarding Max Physics Steps By Frame'

entityPerfNotes:
YES, 2,000+ at 60fps is achievable — but only by deliberately not using Godot the way Godot is taught. This is the make-or-break answer and it is unambiguous.

WHAT DOES NOT WORK: one Node2D / CharacterBody2D / Area2D per entity. Every credible data point converges here. A bullet-hell devlog measured ~230ms per physics step just spawning 20 bullets every 0.1s with per-bullet nodes. A Vampire-Survivors starter kit reportedly saturates around 50 CharacterBody2D enemies, reaching ~200 with Jolt. Godot's own docs say to use the servers API directly once you need thousands of instances. If the agent builds this the tutorial way, it will hit a wall at a few hundred entities and no amount of profiling will save it. This must be written into the spec as a prohibition on day one, exactly like the existing "no `new` inside update()" rule — it is the same class of decision.

WHAT DOES WORK — the concrete recipe:

1. ENTITY STORAGE — structure-of-arrays in PackedFloat32Array / PackedVector2Array / PackedInt32Array, not per-entity objects. These are backed by contiguous native C++ memory and skip GDScript's per-element Variant boxing. This is a direct transposition of the spec's existing pool design: `pool.js` becomes `pool.gd` managing index ranges into packed arrays. Enemies, projectiles, gems, damage numbers, particles all become index-based records. Zero allocation in the hot loop is easier here than in JS, because you pre-size the packed arrays once.

2. COLLISION — do NOT touch PhysicsServer2D or Area2D. Keep the spec's 64px spatial hash exactly as written, implemented over PackedInt32Array buckets, with circle-vs-circle distance checks. Godot's physics is the thing that collapses at these counts; a hand-rolled hash is both faster and gives you deterministic behavior, which the seeded-run requirement needs anyway. This deletes an entire category of engine risk.

3. RENDERING — three options, roughly in order of preference for this game:
   (a) One MultiMeshInstance2D per visual type, driven by set_instance_transform_2d + set_instance_color. GPU-instanced to a single draw call regardless of count. The spec's existing `visual: { shape, color, size, ... }` object maps cleanly onto "which MultiMesh bucket does this entity live in." Best fit for the ~15 enemy archetypes and the bullet swarms.
   (b) RenderingServer.canvas_item_create() + canvas_item_add_texture_rect(), holding RIDs in an array and calling canvas_item_set_transform() per frame. Documented as much faster than equivalent Sprite2D nodes. Watch the RID gotcha: server RIDs are NOT refcounted, so you must hold a reference to the texture outside the server or it gets freed under you.
   (c) A single Node2D whose _draw() loops draw_texture_rect_region() over the entity arrays from one atlas. This is the closest 1:1 port of the spec's `renderer.js` and the easiest for an agent to get right; Godot batches rects sharing texture/material/blend/shader. Start here, escalate to (a) if it measures short.

4. THE MEASURED CEILING — the best public data point is ~240 FPS with 2,500 bullets on an integrated GPU using servers-API shapes plus direct _draw(), versus under 80 FPS with the node approach. That is comfortably above the 2,000-at-60 target with headroom, on hardware weaker than "mid-range laptop." Caveat: it is one devlog, Godot 3-era, and bullets do less per-tick work than this game's enemies (which need AI targeting, status effects, knockback, and separation).

5. THE LANGUAGE MATH — 2,000 entities x 60Hz = 120k entity-updates/sec. At a rough 20-40 VM ops per entity-update, that is 2.4-4.8M ops/sec, well within typed GDScript's budget with packed arrays. Real-time 60fps in GDScript is fine. The 100x headless harness is a different story: 6,000 ticks/sec x 2,000 = 12M entity-updates/sec, ~10-40x the real-time load. GDScript will not do that. Plan for the harness to run at 10-30x in GDScript, or to run a C# desktop build for balance testing only (which then requires the sim core to be language-portable — a real architectural tax), or to push the hot loop into a C++ GDExtension. Decide this before M0, not at M9.

6. NON-NEGOTIABLES for the agent: static type annotations on every variable, parameter and return (up to 59% faster than untyped); no signals, no groups, no get_node(), no `has_method()` duck-typing in the per-entity loop; cache all lookups outside the loop; and Godot 4.6+ specifically, for its bytecode optimizations to array iteration, dictionary access and method-call overhead — the three operations this loop is made of.

7. FREE WIN — the spec's fixed-60Hz-plus-interpolated-render requirement is engine-native (physics interpolation, 2D since 4.3), so the hand-rolled accumulator gets deleted rather than ported. But note: if you go full servers-API, engine physics interpolation does not apply to your custom entities and you interpolate them yourself in the draw pass — which is what the spec already describes. Either way it is not new work.

Bottom line: Godot can hit the number. The cost is that the run-simulation half of the codebase gets essentially none of Godot's ergonomics, tutorials, editor visualization, or LLM training-data advantage. You get Godot's value on the other half — window, input, audio, UI, save, export, console path.
publishingPaths:
This is Godot's strongest category, and it is validated by a game in this exact genre rather than by marketing.

LICENSING FLOOR: MIT. No royalties, no revenue share, no per-seat fee, no install fee, no revenue threshold. You owe an attribution notice in your credits and nothing else, ever. For a game with a monetized gacha layer where revenue could scale unpredictably, this removes a whole category of business risk that Unity's history makes non-theoretical.

DESKTOP (Windows/macOS/Linux): First-class one-click export templates. Steam via GodotSteam (open-source GDExtension, Win/Mac/Linux) or Godot.Steamworks.NET if you go C#. GodotSteam 4.14+ auto-syncs stats and achievements at client boot with no explicit request/callback. Steam has no engine restrictions. Practical cost: macOS needs an Apple Developer ID ($99/yr) for notarization or Gatekeeper blocks your users; Windows code-signing is optional but reduces SmartScreen friction. Brotato and Halls of Torment both proved this path — Brotato at 10M+ copies.

MOBILE (Android/iOS): Native exports, both supported. Halls of Torment shipped Android and iOS in Oct 2024 — direct proof this genre ports. iOS requires a Mac plus Xcode plus the $99/yr Apple account regardless of engine. Worth noting: this game's touch controls (virtual stick + two ability buttons) are already in the spec, so the mobile port is genuinely cheap. For a gacha-flavored anime roguelite, mobile is arguably the natural home, and this is where Godot's story is much better than a browser-only build.

CONSOLE (Switch/Switch 2/PS5/Xbox): A real, walked path. W4 Games sells official middleware export templates for Switch, Switch 2 (early beta as of early 2026), PS5 and Xbox Series X|S, optimized for Godot 4.3+; pricing is per-title/per-platform quotes with nothing published. RAWRLAB released a free Godot port for authorized Nintendo Switch/Switch 2 developers — the zero-cost Switch route. Pineapple Works and Lone Wolf do port-for-hire. Halls of Torment reached PS5 and Xbox in Oct 2025. Caveat: you still need platform-holder dev approval, which is orthogonal to engine choice. Also note the servers-API architecture actually helps here — no node/physics bloat to squeeze onto handheld hardware.

WEB (WASM): The weak link, and the one that should drive the decision. Godot 4 web is WebGL 2.0 / Compatibility renderer only (Forward+/Mobile blocked pending WebGPU), single-threaded by default (threading needs SharedArrayBuffer plus COOP/COEP headers — itch.io sets these for you if you upload a zip). Payload floor is ~35MB compressed WASM for an empty project, ~25MB stripped, before any of your content; Basis Universal texture compression helps assets but not the engine WASM. Godot's own docs state native builds beat web "by a significant margin." And critically, C# cannot export to web at all in Godot 4. Reported WASM heap leakage on long sessions is described as a non-issue under ~30 minutes — this game's 15-25 minute runs plus hub/gacha time sit uncomfortably close to that line and would need testing. Practical verdict: Godot web is fine as an itch.io demo funnel to a Steam page. It is not fine as the primary distribution channel, and it is nothing like the spec's current "open index.html, zero dependencies, offline-playable" premise.

RECOMMENDED SHAPE IF YOU PICK GODOT: Steam-first desktop (that is where Brotato and Halls of Torment made their money in this genre), mobile as the natural second wave given the gacha layer, an itch.io web demo as marketing only, console later via W4 if it sells. That is a strictly better commercial posture than browser-first — but it is a different plan than the spec was written against, and that should be an explicit decision, not a side effect.
portCostFromSpec:
FIRST, THE FACT THAT REFRAMES THIS QUESTION: no code exists yet. The entire repo is `C:\Users\turbo\OneDrive\Documents\GitHub\Gacha Suvivors\GACHA_SURVIVORS_PROMPT.txt` (1,820 lines) plus a `.claude` settings file. There is nothing to port. The "port cost" is purely the cost of editing a design document, and it is small.

QUANTIFIED: Section 1 "TECH STACK & HARD CONSTRAINTS" is lines 161-245 — about 85 lines, ~4.7% of the document. Add roughly 6 scattered engine-coupled lines elsewhere (1657-1658 harness URL, 1690 "canvas", 1717 "index.html", 1726 "browser restart"). Call it ~5% of the spec that needs rewriting. Sections 2-15 and 17-19 — all 19 characters and their 4 ability pillars, 7 stages, the wave director, enemy archetypes, 22 upgrades, 22 relics, the full gacha pity/50-50 math, balance targets, tone guide, the one-to-one ref rule — roughly 1,200 lines, are entirely engine-agnostic and survive verbatim. Section 4 alone (characters, lines 314-930) is 616 lines and does not change by a word.

WHAT SPECIFICALLY CHANGES:

DIES OUTRIGHT: "HTML5 + Canvas 2D, vanilla JavaScript ES modules, no build step, runs by opening index.html, zero external runtime dependencies, offline-playable." Replace with "Godot 4.6.x, statically-typed GDScript (or C# if web is dropped), Compatibility renderer, servers-API entity architecture." Acceptance criterion #1 must be struck entirely — there is no honest Godot equivalent.

SIMPLIFIES (spec gets shorter): The hand-rolled fixed-timestep accumulator is deleted; `_physics_process` at physics_ticks_per_second = 60 with physics interpolation is engine-native since 4.3. The headless harness no longer needs to be invented — `--headless` plus `--disable-render-loop` is a built-in flag. Gamepad support becomes the InputMap rather than the Gamepad API. Net: two hard requirements move from "build this" to "configure this."

MECHANICAL TRANSLATION (same logic, new syntax): The /src tree maps close to file-for-file — rng.js→rng.gd, pool.js→pool.gd, spatialHash.js→spatial_hash.gd, damage.js→damage.gd, and so on. The "ALL content lives in /src/data as plain data objects, adding a character edits exactly ONE file" rule survives intact as either .tres Resources or plain GDScript dictionaries in characters.gd — arguably cleaner in Godot. localStorage becomes FileAccess against user://, and the schemaVersion migration stub is byte-for-byte the same logic. mulberry32/xorshift128 port trivially; keep your own implementation rather than Godot's RandomNumberGenerator so the two-stream run/meta split and anti-save-scum counter stay under your control.

REAL FRICTION, THREE ITEMS:
1. AUDIO. "WebAudio synthesized SFX (square/saw blips, noise bursts, rising arpeggios)" has no direct Godot analogue. AudioStreamGenerator can do it but is clumsier than WebAudio. Better rewrite: synthesize the SFX set once at boot into AudioStreamWAV buffers and play those. Same end result, ~15 lines of spec rewritten.
2. EMOJI PLACEHOLDER ART. Godot supports CBDT/CBLC and SVG color-emoji fonts but not COLR/CPAL, and CBDT blurs above its embedded PNG size. Worse, drawing 2,000 emoji as Label glyphs fights the servers-API render path. The correct rewrite is actually an improvement: bake the emoji set into a texture atlas once at boot and draw from that atlas — which forces the SpriteAtlas drop-in path the spec already wants at line 218, months earlier than planned. Turn a constraint into the intended architecture.
3. HARNESS INVOCATION. `?sim=1&char=rin&stage=2&seed=42` becomes `godot --headless -- --sim=1 --char=rin --stage=2 --seed=42` read via OS.get_cmdline_user_args(). If you keep a web build, JavaScriptBridge can still read location.search, so you can support both forms from one parser. Also: do NOT implement 100x via Engine.time_scale — docs warn precision degrades above 1.0. Use --disable-render-loop and step your own fixed clock, which is more deterministic anyway and matches the seeded-run requirement.

WEAKENED CRITERION: #3, "Zero allocations in the update loop (check with a heap profile)." Godot's profiler is materially worse than Chrome DevTools for this. Restate as "no Object/Array/Dictionary construction inside _physics_process; verify via the Object Count and Memory monitors staying flat across a 5-minute run."

NEW CRITERIA TO ADD: (a) "No entity is a Node — enemies, projectiles, gems, damage numbers and particles exist only as indices into packed arrays." (b) "Every script member, parameter and return is statically typed." (c) A GUT test suite in place of ad-hoc unit tests, since the spec already asks for a unit-tested pity system and a unit-tested one-to-one ref rule — GUT runs headless in CI and this is a straight upgrade over "write a unit test" with no framework named.

HONEST SUMMARY: roughly 90 lines of spec rewritten, two requirements deleted because the engine provides them, one acceptance criterion permanently lost (browser-instant zero-install), three items needing genuine redesign (audio synthesis, emoji atlas, harness invocation), and ~1,200 lines of design content untouched. This is the cheapest moment this decision will ever be — nothing has been built. If Godot is going to be considered at all, it should be decided now, before M0, because the "entities are not Nodes" constraint has to be in the spec from the first line of code.
